sections.heading: Articles and pronouns
sections.sub: The main forms that actually change.

cards.search: the der die das den dem des definite article artikel case

gloss: The man is coming.
I see the man · with the man. der/den/dem all mean “the”; case changes the form.

tiny: English “the” never changes shape — German’s does: the ending is the case marker in action. Bold = the traps of this level: masculine Akkusativ and the whole Dativ column. Genitiv changes too, but A1–B1 needs it less.
Gender is not logic —
is not “she”: learn every noun with its article. Genitiv and Dativ plural also change the noun (
) — see Endings and changes.
Mask. — masculine; Neut. — neuter; Fem. — feminine; Plural — more than one.

cards.search: dieser diese dieses this that demonstrative pronoun

p: Demonstrative: dieser/diese/dieses — this; it can point to “that” in context. Learn the forms with the der/die/das endings; distance is also expressed with hier/dort or jener.

gloss: This man · this woman · this child.
I’m taking this bus. · That’s nice.

cards.search: der ein kein article choice first mention known profession negation

gloss: That is a dog. The dog is big. · That is not a dog.
ein introduces one; der refers to the known one; kein negates.

tiny: Professions normally omit the article when simply naming the job: Ich bin Lehrer — I’m a teacher; Sie ist Ärztin — She’s a doctor. An article can appear with emphasis or qualification: ein guter Lehrer — a good teacher.

cards.search: ein eine einen indefinite kein mein dein sein ihr unser euer possessive possessiv endings

p: English possessives never change (my father, with my father) — German adds the ein-word endings:

gloss: I have a brother and a sister.
With my brother · with my sister.

tiny: Bold = the traps of this level: masculine Akkusativ and the whole Dativ column. Genitiv changes too, but A1–B1 needs it less.
has no plural. The
column is the model for all of them:

tiny.t: kein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer

tiny: take these endings on the same stem.
Mask. — masculine; Neut. — neuter; Fem. — feminine; Plural — more than one.

cards.search: nicht kein negation not no dont where

p: = “not” — everything else (verbs, adjectives, pronouns): the all-purpose negation.

gloss: I don’t have a car. · I’m not sleeping. kein — no/not a; nicht — not.

tiny: German has no do-support: the verb itself is negated — never rebuild “don’t” with a helper verb.

cards.search: personal pronouns ich mich mir du dich dir ihn ihm uns euch ihnen you

p: . German has three forms — and splits English “him” in two.

gloss: Do you know him? — I help him. ihn — Akk.; ihm — Dat. (helfen takes Dativ).

tiny: Bold = the Dativ forms that differ from Akkusativ (uns and euch stay the same).
English has one you; German has three:
· polite
(capital, written like “they” — no English counterpart).

sections.heading: Prepositions
sections.sub: The preposition often decides the case outright.

cards.search: akkusativ prepositions durch für gegen ohne um

gloss: For the man · without me. The preposition fixes the case.

cards.search: dativ prepositions aus bei mit nach seit von zu

gloss: With my brother · to work (zu der → zur). The preposition fixes the case.

cards.search: wechselpräpositionen an auf hinter in neben über unter vor zwischen wo wohin two-way

gloss: On the table (where?) · onto the table (where to?). dem/den show the case.

cards.search: genitiv prepositions wegen trotz während statt innerhalb außerhalb

gloss: Because of the weather. des Wetters — Genitiv of das Wetter (weather).

tiny: In speech some of these also take Dativ, but the norm to learn is Genitiv.

cards.search: warten auf denken an freuen sich teilnehmen verb preposition wait think

p: The preposition almost never matches English:

gloss: I’m waiting for the bus. · He’s thinking about the exam.
Learn the case with the whole pair: warten auf + Akk.; denken an + Akk.

cards.search: seit vor since for ago duration present perfect

p: seit + Dativ — since/for: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier — I have lived here for a year.
vor + Dativ — ago: Ich kam vor einem Jahr — I arrived a year ago.

gloss: I have lived here for two years. · I moved two years ago.
seit — continuing duration; vor — ago.

tiny: For a state continuing now, normally use Präsens: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren hier — I have lived here for two years. seit itself does not rule out Perfekt.

cards.search: hauptsatz main clause statements verb second v2 position 2 word order heute subject

gloss: I’m going to the shop today.
Today I’m going to the shop. gehe — am going; the German finite verb stays in slot 2.

cards.search: inversion fronted adverbs heute dann deshalb position 1 subject verb

h: If the sentence starts with Heute / Dann / Deshalb…

p: …the fronted element takes slot 1 and the subject moves

gloss: Today I have to work. müssen → muss — have to; arbeiten — work.
After Heute the verb comes before ich.

tiny: English keeps “Today I must work” together; German keeps the verb in slot 2 and lets the subject fall behind.

cards.search: questions yes no wer was wann warum wie verb first v1 do support helper

tiny: Kommst du heute? — Are you coming today? · Wann kommst du? — When are you coming?
Yes/no → verb first:
— there is no do-support; no helper verb is inserted.
W-question (wer, was, wann, warum, wie…) → question word + verb — exactly the English pattern.

cards.search: tekamolo temporal kausal modal lokal order adverbs time cause manner place

gloss: I’m travelling to Berlin by train today for work.
heute — today; wegen der Arbeit — for work; mit dem Zug — by train; nach Berlin — to Berlin.

p: A neutral German middle-field order is time–cause–manner–place. English often places time at the end; neither language has one obligatory adverb order.

tiny: A safe default, not a law: emphasis and context can promote time or cause to slot 1.

cards.search: modalpartikeln particles tone doch mal denn ja schon gar wohl just actually probably

p: No literal translation — each one carries
. English does this with intonation and small adverbs; learn the pairs:

gloss: Come here a moment! · That’s obvious, after all! · So, what’s your name?
These are contextual tone clues, not fixed translations.

cards.search: imperative command request komm geht kommen sie sein polite ruhig

p: Use the imperative for requests, commands and instructions: telling someone what to do.
English has one command form for everybody; German picks the form by listener — polite

gloss: Please come along! · Be quiet!
Komm! — come (one familiar person); Geht! — go (several); Kommen Sie! — come (polite).

tiny: sein is irregular here, just like English

gloss: You are waiting (statement). → Please wait! (request). In the imperative form, the verb comes before Sie.

sections.heading: The verb bracket
sections.sub: Part of the verb often lives at the end.

cards.search: modal verbs müssen können wollen sollen dürfen mögen infinitive bracket satzklammer

tiny: Today I have to go to the shop. heute — today; gehen — go; in den Laden — to the shop.

p: opens it, the infinitive closes it — English keeps “must … go” together; German lets the two halves drift apart.

cards.search: perfekt perfect haben sein partizip ii gegangen gemacht past motion

tiny: Ich habe das schon gemacht — I’ve already done that. machen → gemacht — do → done; habe is the Perfekt auxiliary.

gloss: I went home / have gone home (context decides). gehen → gegangen — go → gone; here directed motion to a destination takes sein.

cards.search: trennbare separable verbs prefix bracket aufstehen uhr

tiny: Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf — I get up at 7. aufstehen — get up.

p: The prefix detaches and flies to the end of the bracket — English phrasal verbs keep their particle beside the verb (“I get up at 7”).

gloss: …because I get up at 7. aufstehen — get up; stehe … auf is the separated form.

chips.label: Why whole again in the subordinate clause?

cards.search: passive passiv werden partizip ii gebaut voice

tiny: Das Haus wird 2026 gebaut — The house is being built in 2026. Haus — house; bauen → gebaut — build → built; wird forms the passive.

cards.search: konjunktiv ii würde would wurde unreal conditional polite wäre hätte könnte sollte

p.t: wäre, hätte, könnte, möchte, müsste, sollte

gloss: If I had time, I would travel.
Could you help me? (a polite request).

tiny: Spelling:
(“would”) is not
(“became”).

cards.search: doppelinfinitiv ersatzinfinitiv double infinitive modal perfect haben arbeiten müssen

h: Perfekt with a modal: two infinitives

gloss: I had to work. müssen — have to; arbeiten — work.

tiny: Recognizing it is enough — producing it comes later.

cards.search: präteritum war hatte wollte konnte musste sollte simple past written spoken

p: A second way to talk about the past. Spoken German often prefers Perfekt; written narratives often use Präteritum. sein, haben and modals frequently use Präteritum in speech too.

items.meaning: had to / was supposed to / was allowed to

gloss: I was ill. · I had no time.
sein → war — be → was; haben → hatte — have → had.

tiny: German Perfekt can correspond to English simple past or present perfect: Ich habe gegessen — I ate / I have eaten, depending on context.

sections.heading: Subordinate clauses
sections.sub: Conjunction first, conjugated verb to the end.

cards.search: weil because subordinate verb end clause

tiny: weil ich heute arbeiten muss — because I have to work today.

gloss: I’m not coming because I have to work. kommen — come; müssen — have to; arbeiten — work.

tiny: English keeps its order after “because” — German sends the verb to the end:
is the signature error.

cards.search: dass that subordinate believe think hope say know dropped clause

gloss: I believe he’s coming today. glauben — believe; kommt — is coming/comes.

tiny: Typical after
(believe, think, hope, say, know) — and unlike English “that”, dass is never dropped.

cards.search: wenn if when condition repeated als subordinate

gloss: If I have time, I’ll come. Zeit — time; habe — have; komme — come.

p: If the wenn-clause comes first, the main verb follows the comma — not the subject:

cards.search: obwohl although though subordinate verb end trotzdem

gloss: He’s going for a walk although it’s raining. spazieren gehen — go for a walk; es regnet — it’s raining.

cards.search: ob whether if embedded indirect question wenn

gloss: I don’t know whether he’s coming (an embedded yes/no question). wissen → weiß — know (ich form).

tiny: A condition “if” →
: …, wenn es regnet.

cards.search: und aber denn oder sondern coordinating conjunctions verb second correction

h: Don’t send the verb to the end

gloss: I’m staying at home because I’m tired. denn — because; normal V2 follows.
She’s not from Bucharest but from Deva. sondern — “but” introducing a correction of a negated alternative.

cards.search: um zu damit purpose infinitive subject same different separable

h: um … zu / damit — in order to / so that

gloss: I’m learning German in order to work in Berlin (same subject).
I explain it slowly so that you understand everything (different subjects).

cards.search: relative clause relativsatz der das den dessen deren whose pronoun drop

gloss: That’s the man who works here (der — subject).
That’s the man whom I know (den — object).

tiny: Genitiv: der Mann,
Auto… (“whose”; fem./plural —
English may drop the pronoun (the man I know) — German never does, and the clause’s verb goes last.

cards.search: deshalb trotzdem allerdings außerdem währenddessen linking adverbs therefore nevertheless however besides meanwhile position inversion

legend.label: How do they differ from conjunctions?

gloss: It was raining. So we stayed at home. · Nevertheless, he went for a walk.

tiny: English keeps subject + verb after “therefore”; German inverts: Deshalb blieben wir zu Hause — So we stayed at home. The verb comes before wir.

sections.heading: Endings and changes
sections.sub: Small rules that often break an otherwise correct form.

cards.search: sein haben verb endings present ich du er wir ihr sie arbeiten arbeitest

tiny: Stem + ending: -e, -st, -t (ich/du/er). German conjugates every verb the way English only conjugates be — the table is new, the idea isn’t.
English “you work” ends like “I work” — that’s the trap: not
but

cards.search: dativ plural noun den kindern freunden

p: English nouns have no Dativ ending; German plural nouns normally add -n after den, unless the plural already ends in -n/-s.

gloss: With the children · with my friends. Kind → Kinder — child → children; Freund → Freunde — friend → friends.

cards.search: plural gender umlaut frauen stühle kinder autos loanwords english five patterns

p: Learn the plural with each noun: -e, -er, -(e)n, -s or no ending; sometimes with an umlaut. Gender is a clue, not a reliable prediction.

gloss: Woman → women · chair → chairs.
Child → children · car → cars.

tiny: English comparison: Kind → Kinder adds an ending (child → children); Buch → Bücher also changes the vowel (book → books). Loanwords often take -s: Auto → Autos (car → cars).

cards.search: genitiv possessive vaters hauses english 's

gloss: The father’s car · the colour of the house. Vater — father; Haus — house.

cards.search: n-deklination weak nouns masculine student studenten

p: A group of masculine nouns takes
in every case except Nominativ singular — nothing in English prepares you for it: only

gloss: The student: der Student (subject) → den Studenten (Akk.), dem Studenten (Dat.), des Studenten (Gen.).

cards.search: adjective endings der-words ein-words guter guten

p: English adjectives never change — German endings are pure new territory. The shortcut: after
the article already shows gender and case, so the adjective mostly just echoes

gloss: The good man · with the good man. gut — good; -e/-en are adjective endings.

cards.search: komparativ superlativ comparative superlative als than umlaut besser meisten schnellsten

gloss: It’s warmer today. · I’ll come later than you.
schnell → schneller → am schnellsten — fast → faster → fastest.

tiny: The irregulars are English’s own:
= good–better–the best ·
= much–more–the most ·
= to like better.
= “at the”:
is literally “at the fastest” — English says just “the fastest”.

detail.label: How it works
runs: Find the trigger — a case question, a preposition, a conjunction or a verb construction — then check the form and the verb position.

detail.label: Search
runs: — or in English. Search covers all sections at once.

detail.label: Navigation
runs: Four views at the bottom: cases, forms, word order, subordinate clauses.

detail.label: Words and forms
runs: Modal example: müssen — have to, muss — the ich/er/sie/es form. Infinitiv — base form; Partizip II — participle (machen → gemacht). haben/sein can form Perfekt; werden can form the passive. Translate the whole construction, not each auxiliary literally.

verb-preps.title: Verb + preposition: the pairs
verb-preps.lead: Learn the verb, preposition and case together: warten auf + Akk., teilnehmen an + Dat.

detail.label: The question trick
runs: Who are you waiting for? warten auf takes Akkusativ: Ich warte auf den Bus — I’m waiting for the bus. auf can take Dativ in other constructions; learn this whole pair.
comment: Wen? — whom?; Bus — bus.

detail.label: sich freuen

runs.t: Ich freue mich auf die Reise
Ich freue mich über das Geschenk

comment: I’m looking forward to the trip. · I’m pleased about the gift. Reise — trip; Geschenk — gift.

detail.label: sich
runs: A reflexive pronoun — English has no equivalent (
. For now, recognizing it is enough.
comment: Ich freue mich — I’m pleased / looking forward; du freust dich — you’re pleased / looking forward. mich/dich are reflexive forms with no separate word needed in this English translation.

seit-vor.title: seit: why the present?
seit-vor.lead: For states continuing now, use Präsens; seit marks the starting point or duration.

detail.label: seit = up to now

runs.t: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren hier

runs: ! — see the Dativ plural card). English needs the Present Perfect here; German keeps the present.
comment: I have lived here for two years.

detail.label: vor = ago

runs.t: Ich bin vor zwei Jahren umgezogen

runs: : a finished point in the past + past tense.

detail.label: for and since
runs: seit covers both English words: duration —

detail.label: Not like English

runs.t: I have lived here for two years
Ich wohne hier seit zwei Jahren

runs: . Don’t rebuild the English perfect as Perfekt after seit.

detail.label: The limit
runs: Seit gestern habe ich nichts gegessen.
comment: I haven’t eaten anything since yesterday. Perfekt is possible with seit; the tense follows the intended meaning.

nominativ.title: Nominativ
nominativ.lead: Wer? Was? — the doer, the dictionary form.

detail.label: Usually
runs: The subject — the one doing or being something. English shows it by position (
); German writes it on the article.

detail.label: Example
comment: The man is working. arbeiten — work. Wer arbeitet? — Who works? The doer stands in the Nominativ.

detail.label: Usually
runs: The direct object of the action — in English only the pronoun changes shape (

detail.label: Example
comment: I see the man. sehen → sehe — see (ich form). Wen sehe ich? — Whom do I see?

detail.label: The visible change
runs: never changes shape — this ending is the case marker made visible.

detail.label: Usually
runs: The receiver — the role English marks with
comment: I help the man. Wem helfe ich? — Whom do I help? helfen takes Dativ although English help takes a direct object.

detail.label: Remember

runs.t: mit, bei, nach, seit, von, zu, aus

comment: mit — with; bei — at/with; nach — after/to; seit — since/for; von — from/of; zu — to; aus — out of/from.

detail.label: Usually
runs: Belonging or connection — the job English gives to the possessive ’s.

detail.label: Example
comment: The man’s car. Auto — car; Mann — man. des Mannes ≈ the man’s — English’s other case remnant does the same work.

detail.label: Form
runs: ) — the same -s as the English possessive.
comment: des Mannes — the man’s / of the man. Mann — man; -es is the noun’s Genitiv ending.

wo-wohin.title: Wo? / Wohin?
wo-wohin.lead: The rule behind the two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen).

detail.label: Wo? → Dativ
comment: I am at school. Schule — school.

detail.label: Wohin? → Akkusativ
runs: Direction — the position changes across the boundary:
comment: I am going to school. gehen — go.

detail.label: Important
runs: Not every movement automatically means Akkusativ. Ask: does the position cross the boundary the preposition draws?
comment: I jog in the park (within it) · I jog into the park (direction into it).

objects.title: Two objects
objects.lead: Some verbs take both at once: to whom (Dativ) + what (Akkusativ).

detail.label: These verbs

runs.t: geben, schenken, zeigen, bringen, sagen, erklären…

comment: geben — give; schenken — give as a gift; zeigen — show; bringen — bring; sagen — say; erklären — explain.

detail.label: geben
comment: I give the child the book. Kind — child; Buch — book. I give the child the book — English double-object verbs keep the same two roles; German marks them on the articles.

detail.label: The pattern
runs: Receiver → Dativ, thing handed over → Akkusativ. And where English me/him covers both roles, German splits them: ihn (Akkusativ) vs ihm (Dativ).

detail.label: Examples
comment: For the man · without me · through the town.

detail.label: In practice
runs: See one of these prepositions — the case is already decided; don’t look for a meaning question. English trains the same habit: depend on, wait for — an arbitrary pair to memorize.

prep-dat.title: Dativ prepositions
prep-dat.lead: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu

detail.label: Examples
comment: With my brother · at work · to Berlin.

detail.label: Contractions
comment: zum/zur — to; vom — from / of / about, depending on context.

two-way.title: Wechselpräpositionen
two-way.lead: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen

detail.label: Dativ
comment: The book is lying on the table. liegen — lie/be situated.

detail.label: Akkusativ
runs: Wohin? — the position changes: Ich lege das Buch
comment: I put the book onto the table. legen — put/place.

detail.label: Same split as in / into
runs: (direction). In German the case rides on the question — never on feel.

dieser.title: dieser: declension
dieser.lead: dies- steps in for der/die/das — the endings are the same ones.

detail.label: The model
comment: dieser/diese/dieses — this (also “that” in context); diesen/diesem — case forms.

detail.label: this or that?
runs: dieser normally means “this”: Dieser Tisch — this table. Distance can be specified: dieser Tisch hier — this table here; der Tisch dort — that table over there. jener means “that” but is less common in everyday speech.
comment: dieser Tisch — this table; der Tisch dort — that table over there; jener — that (less common in everyday speech).

detail.label: welcher
comment: Welcher Bus? — Dieser Bus. Which bus? — This bus.

detail.label: dieser or der?
runs: points at one specific thing (“that one there”);
comment: Der Mann ist Lehrer — The man is a teacher. Der Mann dort — The man over there.

detail.label: Adjectives
runs: After dieser an adjective takes the same -e/-en as after der-words — see the Adjectives card in Endings and changes.

article-choice.title: der or ein: first mention or already known
article-choice.lead: First time ein — after that der.

detail.label: The pair

runs.t: Ein Hund läuft durch den Park.

comment: A dog is running through the park. The dog is carrying a ball. laufen — run/walk; tragen — carry. “Some dog” → “the dog we both know” — exactly English a → the.

detail.label: Professions
runs: — no article, the opposite of English “I’m a teacher.”
comment: I’m a teacher. · She’s a doctor. Unmodified professions normally omit the article; emphasis and qualification can license one (ein guter Lehrer — a good teacher).

detail.label: kein
runs: — the negation of that same ein.
comment: That is not a dog but a wolf. Wolf — wolf.

possessives.title: Possessives
possessives.lead: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr

detail.label: Meanings
runs: mein = my · dein = your · sein = his (or its) · ihr = her or their · unser = our · euer = your (plural) ·

detail.label: The owner gives the stem
runs: , with a capital. Small ihr does double duty — her and their; context decides.

detail.label: The ending comes from the table
runs: All of them decline like ein-words: mein Bruder →
→ meines Bruders; any stem works: dein Bruder →
comment: mein Bruder — my brother; meines Bruders — my brother’s.

detail.label: sein = his or its
runs: (his car / its car) — German has no separate “its”.

detail.label: The euer trap
runs: drops its e before an ending: mit
comment: mit eurem Bruder — with your brother; eure Schwester — your sister.

why-ein-endings.title: Why meinen / meinem?
why-ein-endings.lead: The endings are the article’s: den → meinen, dem → meinem, der → meiner.

detail.label: The key
runs: Same endings as the definite article. Compare: den Mann →
comment: Mann — man/husband; meinen Mann — my man/husband (Akk.); meinem Mann — my man/husband (Dat.); meiner Frau — my woman/wife (Dat.).

detail.label: Where there is no ending
runs: Only three cells: Nominativ m/n and Akkusativ n —
. The bare form, like der/das in the article table.
comment: ein Mann — a man; ein Kind — a child.

detail.label: Masculine / neuter, Dativ
comment: ihrem — her/their with a Dativ ending; capital Ihrem — your (polite).

detail.label: Examples
comment: With her/their brother · with her/their child.

detail.label: But
comment: With her/their mother · with her/their friends.

negation.title: nicht: placement
negation.lead: Usually before what remains; right before a word only when you negate that exact word.

detail.label: Before the rest
comment: I’m not coming. · I’m not going to the cinema today. Not pinned to the end — it sits before what’s left of the sentence. Sentence-final only when nothing follows.

detail.label: Before the word
comment: I’m coming not today but tomorrow. “Not today”: you negate the time, not the coming. That “but” is sondern — it only follows a negation.

detail.label: kein declines
runs: Like ein: kein Auto · keine Zeit ·
comment: No car · no time · no man (Akk.) · no child (Dat.).

detail.label: The difference
runs: mein Auto = a car exists, just not mine.

pronouns.title: Personal pronouns
pronouns.lead: Learn the important ones as triplets: Nominativ–Akkusativ–Dativ.

detail.label: Triplets
comment: ich–mich–mir — I–me–to me; du–dich–dir — you–you–to you; er–ihn–ihm — he–him–to him; sie–sie–ihr — she–her–to her; es–es–ihm — it–it–to it. “To” is a role clue, not a fixed translation. English “him” splits in two: ihn (direct object) vs ihm (the “to him” role).

detail.label: Plural
comment: wir–uns–uns — we–us–to us; ihr–euch–euch — you (plural); sie–sie–ihnen — they–them–to them; Sie–Sie–Ihnen — polite you.

detail.label: Genitiv
runs: No personal-pronoun Genitiv here — the forms are rare (statt meiner…) and beyond A1–B1.
comment: statt meiner — instead of me.

conjugation.title: Conjugation: details
conjugation.lead: Stem + ending — but strong verbs change their vowel.

detail.label: -t/-d stems
comment: arbeiten → du arbeitest — work → you work. An -e- is inserted between the -t/-d stem and -st/-t.

detail.label: Vowel change
comment: lesen → du liest — read → you read; fahren → du fährst, er fährt — travel/drive → you travel, he travels. Only du and er change.

detail.label: sein / haben
comment: sein — be: bin/bist/ist — am/are/is; haben — have: habe/hast/hat — have/have/has. Learn them as a table — English be, only busier.

detail.label: wir / ihr / Sie
runs: For regular verbs: wir/sie/Sie match the infinitive; ihr takes stem + -t. sein is an exception: wir/sie/Sie sind, ihr seid.

plural.title: Plural: the five patterns
plural.lead: Five patterns and their meanings; learn each plural with its noun.

detail.label: Feminine
comment: Frau — woman; Zeitung — newspaper; Möglichkeit — possibility.

detail.label: Masculine
comment: Tisch — table; Stuhl — chair; Platz — place/seat.

detail.label: Neuter
runs: Some neuter nouns take -er: Kinder, Bücher, Häuser. Others: das Jahr → die Jahre (year → years), das Fenster → die Fenster (window → windows).
comment: Kind — child; Buch — book; Haus — house. Kind → Kinder adds -er; Buch → Bücher also changes the vowel.

detail.label: Loanwords
runs: , just like English: Autos, Handys, Parks.
comment: Auto — car; Handy — mobile phone; Park — park.

detail.label: No change
runs: Words in -er/-el/-en and -chen/-lein stay as they are (like “sheep”): Lehrer → Lehrer, Fenster → Fenster, Mädchen → Mädchen; sometimes only the vowel moves:
comment: Lehrer — teacher; Fenster — window; Mädchen — girl; Apfel → Äpfel — apple → apples; Vogel → Vögel — bird → birds.

detail.label: Compounds
runs: The plural sits on the last element: das Wörter
comment: Dictionary → dictionaries. Wörterbuch — dictionary.

detail.label: The limit
runs: Gender does not determine the ending. Learn the article, noun and plural together. Dativ plural normally adds -n unless the form already ends in -n/-s.

detail.label: In practice
runs: A useful vocabulary entry: das Buch, die Bücher — book, books; der Tisch, die Tische — table, tables.

detail.label: Common words
runs: Student, Mensch, Junge, Kunde, Kollege, Herr (special form Herrn).
comment: Student — student; Mensch — person/human; Junge — boy; Kunde — customer; Kollege — colleague; Herr — gentleman/Mr.

detail.label: The model
runs: der Student, but den/dem/des Studenten — an
comment: The student: Student changes to Studenten in the other singular cases; its lexical meaning stays the same.

adjectives.title: Adjective endings
adjectives.lead: First ask: does the article already show gender and case?

detail.label: After der-words
runs: Mostly -e or -en — the article has done the work, the adjective echoes it:

runs.t: der gute Mann, den guten Mann, dem guten Mann

comment: The good man: guten in Akk./Dat.; gut — good.

detail.label: After ein-words
runs: When the article shows nothing, the adjective steps in:

runs.t: ein guter Mann, ein gutes Kind
einen guten Mann, einem guten Mann

comment: A good man · a good child; with a good man — mit einem guten Mann.

detail.label: No article
runs: The adjective carries the grammar itself:
comment: Good wine · with good wine. Wein — wine.

detail.label: Scope
runs: This is the compact model, not the full declension table — enough to choose between -e and -en in the common cases.

comparative.title: Comparison: details
comparative.lead: Short adjectives often take an umlaut: kurz → kürzer.

detail.label: Umlaut
comment: Short → shorter; old → older; big/tall → bigger/taller. Usually one-syllable words. English keeps this only as a fossil (foot/feet); German still uses it live.

detail.label: than = als
runs: ich — “bigger than me”. Comparisons always use als; equality is
comment: Bigger/taller than me; so groß wie ich — as tall as me.

detail.label: am -sten
runs: — literally “at the fastest”. With an article: der beste Film.
comment: He runs fastest. · The best film.

v2.title: What “slot 2” means
v2.lead: The verb owns the sentence’s second position — not necessarily the second word.

detail.label: Slot 1 can be a whole phrase
comment: I’m going to work at eight this morning. The whole group “Heute Morgen um acht” fills slot 1 — the verb still comes next.

detail.label: Then the verb, immediately
runs: Nothing can cut in between slot 1 and the finite verb.

detail.label: Compared with English
runs: English never moves the verb (“Today I work at home”); German answers a fronted adverb with inversion:
comment: Heute arbeite ich zu Hause — Today I’m working at home.

tekamolo.title: TeKaMoLo
tekamolo.lead: A useful order for the middle field — not an iron law.

detail.label: The base order

runs.t: Ich fahre heute wegen des Wetters mit dem Bus zur Arbeit

comment: English reshuffles the same facts: “Because of the weather, I’m taking the bus to work today” — time comes last.

detail.label: The predicted error
runs: Ich fahre heute nach Berlin is a neutral order — I’m travelling to Berlin today. Other orders can work with suitable emphasis or context.
comment: Time–cause–manner–place is a useful default, not a test that every alternative is ungrammatical.

detail.label: Why it is not a law
runs: Emphasis, pronouns and definiteness can reorder the middle field. Treat TeKaMoLo as the safe default while you are unsure.

particles.title: Particles: breakdown
particles.lead: Mid-field position — usually right after the verb or the subject.

detail.label: doch
comment: But it’s late, you know. “But it is late, you know”: pushes back against what the other person knows or has just said.

detail.label: ja
comment: That’s obvious, after all. “That’s clear, after all”: obvious to both of you — no proof needed.

detail.label: denn
comment: So, what’s your name? “So what’s your name, then?”: friendly interest, not “why”. Not the conjunction denn — that one lives in Clauses.

detail.label: mal
comment: Come here a moment! “Come here a sec”: softens a request into a nudge.

detail.label: schon / gar
comment: That’s true, I suppose. · That’s not difficult at all. “True, I suppose” (concession) · “not hard at all” (intensifier — almost always with nicht).

detail.label: wohl
comment: He’ll probably come later. “probably”: a cautious guess, no certainty.

detail.label: Position
comment: But I didn’t say anything. After the finite verb or the subject, before the rest — English carries the same nuance with stress: “I did NOT say anything.”

imperative.title: Imperative: forms and word order
imperative.lead: Requests, commands and instructions; the form depends on whom you address.

detail.label: Sie: statement and request
comment: You are waiting. → Please wait! The usual imperative form has verb + Sie. But Sie warten jetzt hier! — “You will wait here now!” — can function as a firm instruction in context; its grammatical form is declarative, not imperative.

detail.label: The du rule
comment: du kommst → Komm! — you come → Come!; du machst → Mach! — you do → Do it!

detail.label: e→i stays, umlaut goes
comment: Gib! — Give!; Lies! — Read!; Fahr! — Drive!/Go! The vowel change survives; the umlaut disappears in the command.

detail.label: -t/-d stems
comment: You wait → Wait! Insert -e-. Pure form learning — English has no parallel here.

detail.label: sein
comment: Be quiet! (one familiar person / several / polite). The exception — and the form you will actually use with strangers: “Be quiet, please.”

detail.label: ihr / Sie
comment: Go! (several familiar people) · Please come! (polite). Sie keeps its place after the verb — a command shape English simply does not have.

modal.title: Modal verbs
modal.lead: können, müssen, wollen, sollen, dürfen, mögen — the bracket construction.

detail.label: Main clause
comment: I have to work today. müssen → muss — must/have to; arbeiten — work. The finite modal takes slot 2, the infinitive goes last. English keeps “must work” adjacent; German spreads the bracket.

detail.label: Subordinate clause
comment: …because I have to work today. Both halves drift to the end — the conjugated modal is the very last word.

detail.label: Negation
comment: nicht müssen — don’t have to (no necessity); nicht dürfen — mustn’t (prohibition).

perfekt.title: Perfekt
perfekt.lead: haben or sein + Partizip II — the everyday spoken past.

detail.label: haben
comment: I worked / have worked, depending on context. German Perfekt and English present perfect overlap, but their uses are not identical.

detail.label: sein
runs: Motion or a change of state with no direct object:
comment: I went / have gone. · He fell asleep / has fallen asleep. gehen — go; einschlafen — fall asleep. Many intransitive verbs of directed movement or change of state take sein.

detail.label: Learn these whole
comment: bleiben — stay; passieren — happen; tanzen — dance.

separable.title: Separable verbs
separable.lead: aufstehen, einkaufen, anrufen… the prefix leaves home.

detail.label: Main clause
comment: I’ll call you later. anrufen — call by phone; später — later. Conjugated stem in slot 2, prefix at the end — the mirror image of English “I’ll call you later”.

detail.label: Infinitive / subordinate clause
comment: anrufen — call; …because I’ll call you later. Nothing takes slot 2, so the verb stays whole and goes to the end.

detail.label: Perfekt
comment: angerufen — called (Partizip II of anrufen). ge- slips in between prefix and stem.

passive.title: The passive in two tenses
passive.lead: werden + Partizip II — and the state reading that English “is built” hides.

detail.label: Present: the event
comment: “The house is being built” — construction is happening. German reserves werden for the event.

detail.label: The state
comment: Das Haus ist gebaut — The house is built (construction is complete). The building is finished — a result with no event. Recognize it; werden is the productive form.

detail.label: The agent
comment: Das Haus wird von einem Architekten gebaut — The house is being built by an architect. “by an architect” = von + Dativ.

detail.label: Perfekt Passiv — recognition
comment: ≈ “The house has been built.” Understand it; do not build it yet.

konjunktiv2.title: Konjunktiv II
konjunktiv2.lead: The unreal, the polite, the advised.

detail.label: würde + Infinitiv
runs: Works for most verbs: Wenn ich Zeit hätte,
comment: Structurally the English conditional: “If I had time, I would read more.”

detail.label: würde with sein / haben
runs: With sein/haben, prefer the direct forms: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, wäre ich froh — If I had time, I would be glad. würde sein/haben can occur in context; it is not universally ungrammatical.
comment: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, wäre ich froh — If I had time, I would be glad. The English habit “if I would have” has no German license: use the direct forms hätte and wäre.

detail.label: Direct forms

runs.t: wäre, hätte, könnte, möchte, müsste, sollte

comment: Ich wäre froh — I would be glad. Du solltest schlafen — You should sleep. wäre — would be; hätte — would have; könnte — could; möchte — would like; müsste — would have to; sollte — should. möchte = “I would like” — the most useful of all.

detail.label: When
comment: Könnten Sie…? — Could you…? Ich hätte gern… — I would like… Du solltest… — You should…

double-infinitive.title: Two infinitives
double-infinitive.lead: Perfekt with a modal — German keeps the modal, English swapped it for had to.

detail.label: The form
runs: haben + Infinitiv + Infinitiv: Ich habe lange
comment: ≈ “I had to work for a long time.” English solved the past modal with a new word —
; German keeps müssen and swaps its participle for an infinitive (not

detail.label: In the subordinate clause
comment: …because I had to work for a long time. haben comes before the two infinitives.

detail.label: Level
runs: Recognizing the construction is enough — you will produce it later.

praeteritum.title: Präteritum: forms
praeteritum.lead: sein, haben and modal verbs often use Präteritum even in speech; Perfekt remains possible.

detail.label: Ready-made forms

runs.t: war, hatte, wollte, konnte, musste, sollte, durfte

comment: war — was; hatte — had; wollte — wanted to; konnte — could; musste — had to; sollte — was supposed to; durfte — was allowed to. Learn as a list — they map straight onto was / had / wanted to / could / had to / should / was allowed to.

detail.label: Regular verbs
comment: machte — did; spielte — played; arbeitete — worked. Understand these; in speech they sound bookish — say Ich habe gearbeitet instead.

detail.label: The Perfekt boundary
comment: Ich bin gegangen — I went / have gone; Er ging — He went. Perfekt can translate either an English simple past or present perfect. Ich musste arbeiten — I had to work.

wenn-als.title: wenn vs als
wenn-als.lead: English “when” covers both — German splits it.

detail.label: als
runs: One specific time in the past:
comment: When I was little / a child… ≈ “when I was a child” — one occasion, closed and gone.

detail.label: wenn

runs.t: Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich.

comment: When(ever) I have time… / If I have time, I’ll come. ≈ “when(ever) I have time, I’ll come.”

detail.label: English “if”
comment: Ich komme, wenn ich Zeit habe — I’ll come if I have time. Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt — I don’t know whether he’s coming. English “if” covers both jobs; German splits them — wenn vs ob.

obwohl.title: obwohl vs trotzdem
obwohl.lead: Both give a contrast, but they build the sentence differently.

detail.label: obwohl
comment: …although it’s raining.

detail.label: trotzdem
runs: Adverb in the main clause → V2: Es regnet.
comment: It’s raining. Nevertheless, I’m going out. The same line English draws between “nevertheless” and “although”.

coordinators.title: weil vs denn
coordinators.lead: Both = “because”, but the word order is different.

detail.label: weil
comment: I’m staying because I’m tired.

detail.label: denn
comment: I’m staying because I’m tired. denn — because; V2 follows. After denn the normal order stays — like after und.

sondern.title: sondern vs aber
sondern.lead: After a negation (nicht, kein) the correction takes sondern — “not A, but B”. A plain contrast without a correction — aber.

detail.label: sondern — the correction
comment: She’s not from Bucharest but from Deva. “not from Bucharest but from Deva”: first negate, then correct to the other option.

detail.label: aber — plain “but”
comment: She’s from Bucharest but lives in Deva. · He likes meat, not fish. Both facts stand; nothing is corrected. Error: Er mag keinen Fisch, aber Fleisch → …, sondern Fleisch (“not fish but meat”).

detail.label: nicht nur …, sondern auch
comment: He speaks not only German but also English. “not only German but also English.”

detail.label: Word order
runs: — normal word order follows: …, sondern sie
comment: …but she lives in Deva.

detail.label: The trigger
runs: English “but” covers both jobs too. The German trigger: a
in front of the corrected part → sondern.
comment: “not A, but B” → sondern; plain “but” → aber.

um-damit.title: um … zu vs damit
um-damit.lead: English makes the same split: in order to vs so that.

detail.label: um … zu
runs: Same subject on both sides: Ich lerne,
comment: ≈ “I’m learning in order to work in Germany.”

detail.label: damit
runs: A full purpose clause: Ich spreche langsam, damit du mich verstehst. Often used when the subjects differ; it is also possible with the same subject.
comment: ≈ “I speak slowly so that you understand me.”

detail.label: zu with separable verbs
comment: aufstehen → aufzustehen — get up → to get up. Es ist schwer, früh aufzustehen — It’s hard to get up early. The prefix jumps in front of zu: “Es ist schwer, früh aufzustehen” ≈ “It’s hard to get up early.”

relative.title: Relative clauses
relative.lead: The relative pronoun is the definite article in disguise: gender and number from the noun, case from its role inside the clause.

detail.label: Nominativ inside
comment: The man who works here… The pronoun is the subject: Wer arbeitet? — der.

detail.label: Akkusativ inside
comment: The man whom I know… The pronoun is the object: Wen kenne ich? — den.

detail.label: Dativ inside
comment: The man whom I help… The receiver: Wem helfe ich? — dem.

detail.label: Genitiv inside
comment: The man whose car is parked there… “whose” (masc./neut.); deren for fem./plural.

linking-adverbs.title: Linking adverbs: the details
linking-adverbs.lead: Position 1, verb right after: Deshalb blieben wir…

detail.label: deshalb / deswegen
comment: I was tired, so I fell asleep immediately. “so / that’s why”: the cause stands in the first sentence.

detail.label: trotzdem vs obwohl
runs: es regnete. — conjunction, verb to the end.
comment: It was raining. Nevertheless, he went out. · …although it was raining. The same line English draws between “nevertheless” and “although”. “Trotzdem, dass…” is colloquial; standard is obwohl.

detail.label: allerdings
comment: The food was good. However, it was expensive. “though / however”: a soft contrast.

detail.label: außerdem
comment: He’s tired. Besides, he has a headache. “besides”: one more thing on the pile.

detail.label: währenddessen
comment: I’m cooking. Meanwhile, he’s watching TV. “meanwhile”: at the same time.

detail.label: Position
runs: : normal order after it — see weil vs denn.
